content: Breast milk can be provided to infants either directly from the mother or through a milk bank. Historically, the use of wet nurses was common, but some women today are uncomfortable with the idea of feeding their child with another woman’s milk. Others, however, value the ability to provide their baby with the benefits of breast milk, even if it is not their own. Feeding expressed breast milk, whether from the baby’s own mother or a donor, is the preferred method for premature infants. The risk of transmitting certain viral diseases through breastfeeding can be mitigated by expressing the milk and subjecting it to Holder pasteurization. Mixed Feeding Predominant or mixed breastfeeding involves feeding breast milk in combination with infant formula, baby food, or even water, depending on the child’s age. Babies feed differently when using artificial teats compared to breastfeeding. When feeding directly from the breast, the baby’s tongue massages the milk out rather than sucking, and the nipple does not go as far into the mouth. In contrast, bottle feeding often requires the infant to suck harder, and milk may flow more rapidly. Introducing bottle feeding or pacifiers before the baby is accustomed to breastfeeding can lead to a preference for the bottle over the breast. Orthodontic teats, which are slightly longer, are designed to mimic the shape of the nipple more closely. Some mothers use alternative methods, such as a small syringe or flexible cup, to supplement feeding and reduce the risk of the baby developing a preference for artificial nipples. Tandem Breastfeeding Tandem breastfeeding refers to nursing two children simultaneously. This is most commonly seen in the case of twins, but it can also occur when a mother continues to nurse an older child while breastfeeding a younger one. Since each child may have different appetites and feeding habits, the mother may need to feed them according to their individual needs. This can include breastfeeding them together, with one child on each breast. For mothers of triplets or more, managing feeding schedules to meet the demands of all the babies can be challenging. While the breasts can adapt to produce large quantities of milk, many mothers use supplemental feeding methods. However, some mothers have successfully breastfed triplets. Tandem breastfeeding can also occur when a woman becomes pregnant while still nursing an older child. During the later stages of pregnancy, the milk transitions to colostrum, which may lead some older children to wean due to changes in taste or supply, while others may continue nursing. Breastfeeding during pregnancy is considered a form of tandem feeding, as the mother provides nutrition for both the nursing child and the developing fetus. Advocates of extended breastfeeding believe that the nutritional, immunological, and emotional benefits of human milk persist as long as the child continues to nurse. Older children who continue to nurse often do so infrequently or sporadically as a way to bond with their mother. Shared Breastfeeding Shared breastfeeding, where more than one woman breastfeeds a child, was historically common worldwide and remains so in some developing nations, such as those in Africa. However, shared breastfeeding poses a risk of HIV transmission to infants. A woman who breastfeeds another’s baby is referred to as a wet nurse. In Islamic tradition, the relationship between the wet nurse and the infants she nurses is codified, and milk siblings are considered equivalent to blood siblings, meaning they cannot marry. In the Anglosphere, shared breastfeeding can provoke strong negative reactions. For example, American feminist activist Jennifer Baumgardner has written about her experiences with this issue in New York. Weaning Weaning is the process of introducing an infant to other foods while gradually reducing the supply of breast milk. Complete weaning occurs when the infant relies entirely on other foods for nutrition and no longer receives breast milk. Most mammals stop producing the enzyme lactase after weaning, leading to lactose intolerance. However, many humans have a genetic mutation that allows lactase production to continue throughout life, enabling them to consume milk—typically cow or goat milk—well beyond the weaning age. In the past, the drug bromocriptine was sometimes used to alleviate breast engorgement during weaning, but the FDA withdrew this indication for the drug in 1994. History of Breastfeeding Before the 20th century, alternatives to breastfeeding were rare. Attempts in 15th-century Europe to use cow or goat milk were largely unsuccessful. In the 18th century, flour or cereal mixed with broth was introduced as a substitute for breast milk, but this also yielded poor outcomes. True commercial infant formulas became available in the mid-19th century, but their widespread use did not occur until after World War II. As the superior qualities of breast milk became more established in medical literature, breastfeeding rates increased, and many countries enacted measures to protect the rights of infants and mothers to breastfeed. Sociological Factors in Breastfeeding Research has identified several social factors that influence the initiation, frequency, and duration of breastfeeding practices among mothers. Race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and other factors have been shown to affect a mother’s decision to breastfeed and the length of time she continues to do so. Education: Mothers with higher levels of education are more likely to breastfeed and to do so for longer durations. Race and Culture: African American women are less likely to breastfeed compared to white women of similar socioeconomic status, while Hispanic women are more likely to breastfeed. This suggests that cultural acceptance of breastfeeding may be linked to socioeconomic status within a given culture. Income: Women and children who qualify for the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) are among the least likely to initiate breastfeeding. Lower income levels can also contribute to early discontinuation of breastfeeding. More highly educated women are often better informed about breastfeeding challenges and are more likely to continue breastfeeding despite difficulties. Women in higher-status jobs are more likely to have access to lactation rooms and face less social stigma for breastfeeding or expressing milk at work. Conversely, women who cannot take extended leave from work after childbirth are less likely to continue breastfeeding upon returning to work.
